lead: An electronic ignition system replaces the contact breaker with a sensor and a transistor. The transistor switches the coil primary current, and an electronic module or the engine ECU decides when to start that current and when to stop it. Programmed ignition goes further: it stores spark advance and dwell in look-up maps indexed by engine speed and manifold pressure (or air flow), then adds corrections for coolant temperature, knock and starting. You meet it on almost every petrol car and motorcycle sold today.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the coil and primary circuit, Chapter 2.2 for spark voltage, and crank position sensors from Unit 3.

sections.h3: From points to a transistor switch

blocks.text: The contact breaker is a mechanical switch driven by the camshaft. A rubbing block opens the points, the primary current falls, and the coil makes the high-voltage pulse. Three problems appear as engines get faster. The points burn because they interrupt several amperes many times a second. The dwell angle drifts as the rubbing block wears, so coil current changes. At high speed the points may not stay closed long enough to build full current.

Electronic ignition removes the rubbing block. A magnetic reluctance or Hall-effect pick-up on the crankshaft or distributor sends a pulse each time a trigger wheel tooth passes. The pulse tells the module the crank angle. The module drives a power transistor, often called the igniter, in series with the coil primary. The transistor does the switching; the pick-up only reports position. A small signal from the pick-up controls a large current in the coil.

Dwell control is the next step. Dwell is the time the primary current is allowed to flow before the spark. In a constant-dwell system the module keeps the dwell time nearly fixed, so the coil gets the same charging time at every speed. In a constant-energy system the module measures battery voltage and coil current and adjusts dwell to reach a target energy before each spark. At low battery voltage it lengthens dwell; at very high speed the time between sparks becomes too short, so it must shorten dwell and accept less than the target energy.

blocks.where: f<sub>spark</sub> is sparks per second; N is engine speed in rev/min; z is number of cylinders; T<sub>spark</sub> is the time between sparks in seconds; D is dwell as a fraction of the spark period; t<sub>dwell</sub> is dwell time in seconds. The z/2 factor applies to a four-stroke engine, which sparks once per two revolutions per cylinder.

blocks.text: At 5000 rpm a four-cylinder four-stroke engine makes 166.7 sparks/s, so each spark period is 6 ms. A dwell fraction of 0.60 then gives 3.6 ms of primary current.

Programmed ignition, also called electronic spark advance or digital ignition, stores the spark timing in a look-up table inside the ECU. The table has engine speed on one axis and manifold pressure or air flow on the other. Each cell holds a spark advance in degrees before top dead centre (BTDC). The ECU reads the cell for the current speed and load, then adds corrections. Coolant temperature correction gives extra advance when the engine is cold or reduces it while warming. Knock correction retards the spark in small steps when the knock sensor reports detonation, then returns advance slowly. Starting correction fixes a safe advance during cranking.

The chain has seven blocks. A crank sensor gives speed and crank angle. A knock sensor gives a retard request. The ECU holds the map and calculates dwell and timing. The ignition driver, or igniter, switches the primary current. The coil stores energy and makes the high voltage, typically around 25 kV. The distributor sends that voltage to the correct plug in the firing order. On a four-cylinder engine the order may be 1-3-4-2. Later systems remove the distributor, as Chapter 2.4 explains.

The ECU sends a dwell pulse to the igniter. The leading edge starts primary current; the trailing edge stops it and fires the spark. The time between the two edges is the dwell time. The angle between the trailing edge and top dead centre is the spark advance. Both are computed, so the same engine can use different values for idle, cruise and full load.

Four control methods appear in order of increasing freedom. Mechanical control uses centrifugal and vacuum advance; it cannot correct for temperature. Electronic control replaces points with a transistor but may still use a fixed advance curve. Mapped control uses a table in memory, so the advance can follow any shape the calibrator chooses. Closed-loop knock control adds feedback: the knock sensor listens for detonation, the ECU retards timing, and then advances it back until knock reappears. This lets the engine run near the knock limit without damage.

The driver sees the result as smooth idle, clean acceleration and no pinging under load. The service technician sees it as a scan tool data stream: rpm, manifold pressure, coolant temperature, calculated advance, knock retard and dwell. A faulty crank sensor usually stops the spark; a faulty knock sensor usually forces a default retard.

figure.caption: The crank sensor reports speed and angle to the ECU; the ECU turns that into a dwell pulse for the igniter, and the coil, distributor and plugs deliver the spark in firing order. The knock sensor can pull timing back when detonation starts.

examples.question: A four-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine runs at 5000 rpm. The ignition system holds a dwell of 60% of the spark period. A knock sensor requests 4° of spark retard. Find the spark rate in sparks per second, the spark period, the dwell time, and the time taken by 4° of crank rotation.
steps: Engine speed N = 5000 rev/min. Number of cylinders z = 4. For a four-stroke engine, sparks per second f = (N/60) × (z/2) = (5000/60) × (4/2) = 83.333 × 2 = 166.667 sparks/s.
Spark period T = 1/f = 1/166.667 s = 0.006 s = 6 ms.
Dwell fraction D = 0.60. Dwell time t = D × T = 0.60 × 6 ms = 3.6 ms.
One revolution takes 60/5000 s = 0.012 s = 12 ms. That covers 360°. So 4° of crank takes 4 × 12/360 ms = 0.133 ms.
examples.answer: Spark rate is 166.7 sparks/s, spark period is 6 ms, dwell time is 3.6 ms, and 4° of crank rotation takes 0.133 ms.
examples.check:
N = 5000
z = 4
D = 0.60
retard = 4
f = (N/60) * (z/2)
T = 1 / f
t_dwell = D * T
rev_time = 60 / N
t_retard = retard * rev_time / 360
print(round(f, 1))
print(round(T * 1000, 1))
print(round(t_dwell * 1000, 1))
print(round(t_retard * 1000, 3))

traps: Treating dwell as a fixed angle at all speeds. With points, the dwell angle is fixed, so the dwell time shrinks as speed rises and the coil may not reach full current. An electronic constant-dwell system fixes the dwell time instead, and a constant-energy system varies the dwell time so each spark reaches a target coil energy.
Mixing spark advance with dwell. Advance is when the spark occurs relative to top dead centre; dwell is the charging time before that spark.
Forgetting the z/2 factor for a four-stroke engine. Using N/60 alone gives one spark per revolution, not one spark per two revolutions per cylinder.
Reading the map axis as accelerator pedal position. Many advance maps use manifold pressure or air flow, not pedal angle.
Assuming knock retard is permanent. The ECU retards timing only while knock is present, then advances back toward the mapped value.

quiz.q: What is dwell in an ignition system?
quiz.a: Dwell is the time the primary current flows in the ignition coil before the spark. It is measured in milliseconds or as a fraction of the spark period.

quiz.q: Why did electronic ignition replace the contact breaker?
quiz.a: The points burn because they switch several amperes. Their dwell angle drifts as the rubbing block wears. At high speed they may not stay closed long enough for full coil current. A transistor and a position sensor avoid all three problems.

quiz.q: A six-cylinder four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm. Dwell is 50% of the spark period. Find the spark period and dwell time.
Why can a constant-dwell electronic ignition still lose spark energy at very high speed?
quiz.a: With constant dwell time the coil gets a fixed charging time, but the spark period falls as speed rises. If the available time between sparks becomes shorter than the required dwell, the driver must shorten dwell. Coil current then falls before the target energy is reached.

quiz.q: Name two pick-ups used in electronic ignition to replace the contact breaker.
quiz.a: Magnetic reluctance pick-up and Hall-effect pick-up.

quiz.q: Which corrections are added to the base spark advance map?
quiz.a: Coolant temperature correction, knock retard correction, and starting correction. Some systems also correct for battery voltage and air temperature.

quiz.q: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine runs at 4000 rpm. How much time does 5° of crank rotation take?
quiz.a: One revolution takes 60/4000 s = 0.015 s = 15 ms. 5° takes 5 × 15/360 ms = 0.208 ms.

quiz.q: Compare mapped ignition control with closed-loop knock control.
quiz.a: Mapped control reads a stored advance value for the current speed and load but does not check the result. Closed-loop knock control adds a knock sensor: it retards timing when detonation is detected and advances back slowly. Mapped control is open loop; knock control is feedback around the knock limit.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines now use ion-sensing ignition, where the spark plug itself measures combustion ions after the spark. Individual-cylinder knock control and model-based calibration are common in research. Coil-on-plug and 48 V mild-hybrid systems change the dwell budget. Search for 'ion current sensing ignition', 'individual cylinder knock control' and 'model-based spark calibration'.
